CEST-detectable metabolite candidates: pancreas

0 of 6 candidates clear the simulated with-vs-without contrast threshold (0.5%) at some field strength, by chemical exchange (downfield, +ppm) or by the relayed NOE (upfield, −ppm). 3 fall below it; 3 are unknown because no group had a verified reference rate, so nothing could be simulated. The threshold applies to our own simulation, never to a literature MTRasym.

Individual molecules within it (free choline, phosphocholine, glycerophosphocholine) do not individually reach >1 mM in the abstracts reviewed.; [model's own exclusion] Glutamate: Identified in mouse pancreas NMR (PMID 23864784) but no absolute concentration found in available abstracts; likely <3 mM but no source.; [model's own exclusion] Glutamine: Detected in some pancreas metabolomics but no absolute concentration found.; [model's own exclusion] Leucine/isoleucine/valine (BCAAs): Detected in NMR but no absolute concentration found.; [model's own exclusion] Creatine/phosphocreatine: Very low in pancreas; no data found.; [model's own exclusion] N-acetylaspartate (NAA): Neuronal marker; not present in pancreas at meaningful levels.; [model's own exclusion] Mobile protein/peptide amide pool (APT): Undoubtedly present in pancreas as in all tissues, but no quantitative pancreas-specific concentration found in any retrieved abstract; general brain APT values (~200-300 mM amide-proton-equivalent in gray matter) are brain-specific and cannot be extrapolated to pancreas.; [model's own exclusion] Glycosaminoglycans (gagCEST): Not physiologically relevant to pancreas parenchyma; cartilage/disc only.; [model's own exclusion] ATP/ADP/AMP: Present in all cells but primarily 31P MRS targets; no 1H CEST literature for pancreas; exchangeable protons limited; no concentration data found in search results.; [model's own exclusion] Phosphomonoesters/phosphodiesters: Spectroscopic category labels, not single molecules - excluded by rules.

glycogen (glucosyl-unit pool) — CEST: ✗ not detectable

Concentration: 0.30 mM typical (0.1-0.8 mM) animal evidence only

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: Glycogen concentration is reported here as mM of glucosyl-unit-equivalent (the repeating unit), not as intact macromolecule molarity. Liver glycogen in fed rats is ~200-400 mM glucosyl units; skeletal muscle is ~80-100 mM glucosyl units. Pancreas has negligible glycogen stores. Based on rat data (PMID 30067510), pancreas glycogen is <1% of liver levels. Taking liver as ~300 mM gives ~0.3 mM glucosyl-unit concentration in pancreas. Each internal glucosyl unit has 3 exchangeable hydroxyl (-OH) protons. At ~0.3 mM glucosyl units, the exchangeable-proton-pool concentration is ~0.3 mM × 3 = 0.9 mM hydroxyl-proton-equivalent. This is too low for useful CEST contrast.

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (hydroxyl OH (O2,O3,O6) [hydroxyl]: concentration 0.1-0.8 mM, kex fixed at 31850 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown); aliphatic C-H (rNOE, glycoNOE) [rnoe]: concentration 0.1-0.8 mM, kex fixed at 5 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown)) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.00-0.00%, 1.5 T: 0.00-0.01%, 3 T: 0.00-0.01%, 5 T: 0.00-0.02%, 7 T: 0.00-0.02%. Threshold 0.5%.

Frequency-collision analysis: Hydroxyl (+1.0 ppm) severely overlaps with lactate hydroxyl (+0.75 ppm) at all fields: separation 5.3 Hz at 0.5 T, 16 Hz at 1.5 T, 31.9 Hz at 3 T, 53.2 Hz at 5 T, 74.5 Hz at 7 T; combined exchange-broadened linewidth ~5196 Hz dwarfs all separations. rNOE (−1.1 ppm) collides with semisolid MT (−2.4 ppm) at all fields: separation 83-387 Hz vs linewidth ~15937 Hz — completely blurred.

Direct water saturation: Hydroxyl at +1.0 ppm sits within or at the edge of the direct saturation bandwidth at 0.5 T (offset ~21 Hz, bandwidth 4.3 Hz) and 1.5 T (offset ~48 Hz, bandwidth 21.3 Hz) — severely masked. rNOE at −1.1 ppm is further from water and less affected.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: Hydroxyl kex 31850 s⁻¹ from PMID 38933551 — measured in phantom/solution (in vitro glycogen), not in vivo, not in pancreas. rNOE kex 5 s⁻¹ from PMID 25996515 — generic class value from protein phantoms, not from glycogen. Both exchange rates are unverified for in vivo pancreas and may differ substantially.

Caveats / critique (7 points, 324 words) — Agent 1's 0.3 mM glucosyl-unit-equivalent concentration likely overestimates pancreatic glycogen. Pancreas has minimal glycogen storage — essentially none in ex…
  • Agent 1's 0.3 mM glucosyl-unit-equivalent concentration likely overestimates pancreatic glycogen. Pancreas has minimal glycogen storage — essentially none in exocrine tissue, trivial in islets. Liver (100-500 mM glucosyl units) and muscle (50-100 mM) are the glycogen stores. Even at 0.3 mM, contrast reaches only 0.009%.
  • Agent 2 correctly identifies: (1) three hydroxyl groups per glucosyl unit — class hydroxyl, correct; (2) seven aliphatic C-H ring protons — class rnoe (glycoNOE), correct. I agree with both class assignments. No exchangeable protons were neglected.
  • Hydroxyl shift 1.0 ppm and rNOE shift −1.1 ppm in the simulation are consistent with literature values from muscle and liver (PMID 19358232, PMID 36161668, PMID 39529314). No evidence of in vivo shift differences for pancreas specifically. None — all three hydroxyls and seven aliphatic C-H per glucosyl unit were accounted for.
  • verifying_citations: PMID 19358232 (claimed as 'In vivo 3 T magnetic resonance imaging and spectroscopy of human muscle glycogen.') dropped PubMed's actual title is 'Water saturation shift referencing (WASSR) for chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST) experiments.'. verifying_citations: PMID 36161668 (claimed as 'Free-breathing 3D abdominal chemical exchange saturation transfer imaging with MR multitasking.') dropped
  • PubMed's actual title is 'Free-breathing 3D CEST MRI of human liver at 3.0\xa0T.'. no SAR or hardware ceiling is applied: the recommended B1/Tsat is the sweep optimum, and deliverability must be checked against the scanner's SAR monitor Pancreas glycogen is very low.
  • The exchangeable-proton-pool concentration for glycoCEST is ~0.9 mM hydroxyl-proton-equivalent (0.3 mM glucosyl units × 3 -OH per unit), far below the concentration needed for reliable CEST contrast. Animal evidence only.
  • [Eligibility] typical_concentration_mM (0.3 mM) looks like the intact macromolecule's own molarity rather than its exchangeable-proton pool concentration -- this survived the re-emission check meant to catch it, so the simulated contrast for this metabolite is likely a severe underestimate. [Unsourced reasoning] 1 numeric step(s) rest on an unsourced assumption: 'Estimate pancreas glycogen as ~0.1% of liver glucosyl-unit concentrati'.

glutathione (GSH) — CEST: ✗ not detectable

Concentration: 2.50 mM typical (1.0-4.0 mM) animal evidence only

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: Glutathione is a defined small molecule (tripeptide) present in virtually all mammalian tissues. Rat pancreas GSH is discussed in the hyperlipidemia study (PMID 18067231) with GSH measurements in plasma and pancreas tissue, though absolute mM values in pancreas are not in the abstract. Typical mammalian intracellular GSH is 1-10 mM. Liver GSH is 5-8 mM (textbook). Pancreas GSH is reported as 30-50% of hepatic levels across species. I estimate pancreas GSH at 2.5 mM. GSH has 4 exchangeable protons per molecule: 1 thiol (-SH), 2 backbone amides, 1 free amine (-NH₃⁺). Exchangeable-proton-pool concentration = 2.5 mM × 4 = 10 mM.

Robustness to input uncertainty: no

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (amide NH (gamma-Glu-Cys backbone) [amide]: concentration 1-4 mM, kex 15-158 s−1) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.00-0.03%, 1.5 T: 0.01-0.08%, 3 T: 0.01-0.16%, 5 T: 0.01-0.23%, 7 T: 0.01-0.26%. Threshold 0.5%.

Frequency-collision analysis: At 0.5 T, amide (+3.5 ppm) collides with glycogen hydroxyl (+1.0 ppm) — separation 53.2 Hz vs combined linewidth ~5111 Hz — completely blurred. At 1.5-7 T, separation grows (159.7-745.1 Hz) but remains far smaller than the exchange-broadened linewidth (~5111 Hz). The amide is in slow exchange with water, but MTRasym at 3.5 ppm will contain hydroxyl and MT contributions from other pools.

Direct water saturation: Amide at +3.5 ppm is well outside the direct saturation bandwidth at all fields (bandwidth 21.3-31.9 Hz, offset 75-1493 Hz depending on field). No direct-saturation masking of the amide signal.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: Amide kex of 65.5 s⁻¹ is the median of 15 s⁻¹ and 116 s⁻¹ — both from generic amide measurements in human brain (PMIDs 40228056, 23008121), not from GSH, not from pancreas. The amine and thiol groups are marked NOT SIMULATED — UNKNOWN; no contrast can be claimed for them.

Potential clinical impact

No verified disease application of this pool's CEST/NOE signal was found. Queried: glutathione CEST pancreas (0), glutathione MRS pancreas (0), glutathione pancreas diabetes (8, all biochemical). No CEST or MRS study of GSH in pancreas found.

Caveats / critique (8 points, 397 words) — Agent 1's concentration of 2.5 mM is plausible. Brain GSH is 1-3 mM, liver 3-5 mM. Pancreas likely falls in 1-3 mM range. The uncertainty range (1-4 mM) is adeq…
  • Agent 1's concentration of 2.5 mM is plausible. Brain GSH is 1-3 mM, liver 3-5 mM. Pancreas likely falls in 1-3 mM range. The uncertainty range (1-4 mM) is adequate. No significant issue.
  • Agent 2 correctly identifies: (1) two backbone amide NH groups — class amide, correct; (2) amine NH₃⁺ (N-terminus) — class amine, correct; (3) thiol SH — class thiol, correct. I agree with all class assignments. Both amides at ~3.5 ppm is plausible for backbone amides. No exchangeable protons were neglected.
  • The simulated amide shift of 3.5 ppm matches the standard APT/amide CEST frequency reported in liver and brain (PMIDs 26334509, 26391991, 32785767). No pancreas-specific in vivo amide frequency measurement was found. None — all four exchangeable groups (two amides, one amine, one thiol) were identified by the chemist.

lactate — CEST: ✗ not detectable

Concentration: 1.50 mM typical (0.5-3.0 mM) animal evidence only

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: Lactate is a defined small molecule identified as a major metabolite in normal mouse pancreas by HRMAS 1H NMR (PMID 23864784). Typical tissue lactate in normoxic mammalian tissues is 0.5-2 mM (Geigy Scientific Tables). The abstract notes that lactate was among metabolites increased in pancreatic cancer vs normal pancreas, consistent with its presence in normal tissue at moderate concentration. I estimate pancreas lactate at 1.5 mM. Lactate has 1 exchangeable hydroxyl (-OH) proton per molecule. Exchangeable-proton-pool concentration = 1.5 mM × 1 = 1.5 mM, which is marginal for CEST.

Frequency-collision analysis: At 0.5 T, lactate hydroxyl (+0.75 ppm) severely overlaps with glycogen hydroxyl (+1.0 ppm) — separation 5.3 Hz vs combined linewidth ~5196 Hz — completely unresolved. At 1.5-7 T, separation is 16-74.5 Hz vs ~5196 Hz; never resolves. At 0.5 T, also collides with glycogen rNOE (−1.1 ppm) at 39.4 Hz vs 128 Hz. At 1.5 T, collides with rNOE (118.1 Hz vs 128.1 Hz). Semisolid MT collision present at all fields.

Direct water saturation: At 0.5 T: direct saturation bandwidth 4.3 Hz, lactate offset ~16 Hz — severely masked. At 1.5 T: bandwidth 21.3 Hz, offset ~48 Hz — partially masked. At 3 T: bandwidth 21.3 Hz, offset ~96 Hz — less masked. At 5-7 T: bandwidth 42.6 Hz, offset 160-224 Hz — better but not clean.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: Hydroxyl kex of 600 s⁻¹ is borrowed from PMID 20951217 — a myo-inositol measurement in human brain, not from lactate, and not from pancreas. The true lactate hydroxyl kex at pH 7.4, 37°C is likely ~10⁵ s⁻¹ (faster), which would produce even broader, weaker CEST contrast. The shift of 0.75 ppm from PMID 35645392 is from a human study including in vivo post-exercise data — this shift is reliable.

In vivo verification: ROI-differential CEST scan — Axial, tilted to match the long axis of the pancreatic body at L1/L2 level

Why this scan: An axial slab through the pancreatic body simultaneously contains pancreas (target), liver, spleen, and paraspinal muscle. These tissues differ in known concentrations of GSH, lactate, glycogen, taurine, alanine, and zinc. If an observed Z-spectrum contrast at a metabolite's offset correlates with its known concentration gradient across ROIs, that pattern confirms the metabolite's contribution rather than generic MT/NOE.

ROIWhere it is drawnRole
pancreatic body target tissueEntire cross-section of the pancreatic body visible on the axial slab, drawn freehand within the organ margin excluding peripancreatic fatTarget tissue; contains beta-cell-rich islets with high zinc and high taurine; moderate GSH and alanine
liver (right lobe)2-cm-diameter circle in right hepatic lobe segment VII/VIII, avoiding large vessels and bile ductsComparison tissue; highest GSH of any solid organ; highest glycogen; moderate taurine and alanine
spleen1.5-cm-diameter circle in splenic parenchyma, avoiding hilar vesselsComparison tissue; high taurine; moderate GSH; low glycogen; negligible zinc
paraspinal muscle1-cm-diameter circle in erector spinae muscle group, avoiding macroscopic fat streaksComparison tissue; very low GSH and glycogen; highest lactate at rest; high taurine; moderate alanine; no zinc

Scan protocol: 3 T, rectangular hard pulse train, B1=0.5 µT, 120 pulses × 20 ms (interpulse delay 5 ms, duty cycle 80%), total Tsat=3000 ms, TR=3600 ms

SAR reasoning (the experimentalist agent's own; the pipeline applies no SAR model): 120 pulses of 20 ms at 0.5 µT with 80% duty cycle over 3 s yields a time-averaged B1 of ~0.4 µT. At 3 T this corresponds to ~0.15 W/kg whole-body average, well below the IEC 60601-2-33 first-level controlled limit of 2 W/kg. The long TR (3.6 s) and centric GRE readout provide further cooling. Respiratory gating adds dead time that reduces duty cycle further.

Compromise rationale:

  • GSH amide (3.5 ppm, slow exchange) would ideally need ~0.75 µT but still saturates at 0.5 µT with 3 s Tsat. Amine pools (GSH amine at 2.95 ppm, taurine at 2.95 ppm, alanine at 2.2 ppm) are near-optimal at 0.5 µT.
  • Glycogen OH (1.0 ppm) and its rNOE at -1 ppm are oversaturated at 0.5 µT (ideal ~0.25 µT), but residual contrast may survive. Lactate OH (0.8 ppm, fast exchange) is undersaturated. The compromise favours GSH and amine pools at the expense of glycogen and lactate. Zinc ions have no exchangeable protons and produce no CEST signal regardless of B1.

Fat suppression: SPAIR prepulse optimised for fat at 3 T (~170 ms inversion time) applied before each saturation train. Pancreas is surrounded by retroperitoneal and visceral fat; SPAIR nulls lipid signal at 1.2 ppm, reducing fat artefacts in Z-spectra. A water-selective 1-3-3-1 binomial excitation is added as backup if SPAIR alone is insufficient. Fat suppression is essential because peripancreatic fat would contaminate the pancreatic body ROI.

Motion mitigation: Respiratory triggering using a pneumatic belt navigator at the diaphragm dome with acceptance window at end-expiration (~40% duty cycle). Free-breathing acquisition; each offset requires ~9 s. Total scan time for 36 offsets x 2 averages: ~10.8 min. Glucagon (0.5 mg IM, contraindication-checked) is administered to reduce duodenal peristalsis adjacent to the pancreatic head. No swallowing issues in the upper abdomen.

Slice coverage: Single 8-mm axial oblique slab centred at the L1/L2 intervertebral disc level, tilted approximately 15 degrees craniocaudally to match the long axis of the pancreatic body as seen on a coronal localiser. The slab extends from the right hepatic lobe (segment VII/VIII) through the splenic hilum, capturing the pancreatic body in its mid-portion. The slab prescription is checked against a breath-hold coronal localiser to ensure the pancreas is fully within the slab.

Structures in FOV: pancreas, liver, spleen, paraspinal muscle, right kidney (lower pole), perirenal fat, retroperitoneal fat, aorta, inferior vena cava, duodenum, vertebral body (L1)

Differential analysis plan:

  • After acquisition, Z-spectra from each ROI are averaged and normalised to the mean of the far-off-resonance baselines (±5, ±6 ppm). B0 inhomogeneity correction is applied using the WASSR map.
  • For each metabolite, MTRasym is computed at its characteristic offset: MTRasym(3.5 ppm) for GSH amide; MTRasym(2.95 ppm) for GSH amine + taurine; MTRasym(2.2 ppm) for alanine; MTRasym(0.8 ppm) for lactate OH; MTRasym(1.0 ppm) for glycogen OH. For glycogen rNOE at -1 ppm, MTR_Rex is used.
  • The pattern across ROIs is compared to the known concentration gradient: GSH should be liver > pancreas ≈ spleen > muscle lactate should be muscle > pancreas ≈ spleen ≈ liver glycogen OH should be liver > muscle >> pancreas ≈ spleen taurine should be spleen > muscle > pancreas ≈ liver
  • alanine should be liver > muscle > pancreas ≈ spleen. If the measured contrast follows the concentration gradient for a given metabolite, that confirms its contribution. If all ROIs show similar contrast despite differing concentrations, the signal is a non-specific MT/NOE effect.

Not actively targeted: Zinc ions (Zn²⁺) in beta-cell secretory granules have no exchangeable protons and produce no direct CEST signal. They are included in the organ_predictions for completeness with zero expected contrast. All other metabolites (GSH, lactate, glycogen, taurine, alanine) are actively targeted.

Caveats (6 points, 247 words) — Pancreas is a small, mobile organ surrounded by bowel gas and retroperitoneal fat. ROI partial-volume effects are significant even with an 8-mm slab. B0 inhomog…
  • Pancreas is a small, mobile organ surrounded by bowel gas and retroperitoneal fat. ROI partial-volume effects are significant even with an 8-mm slab. B0 inhomogeneity from bowel gas and the vertebral body may exceed 0.2 ppm across ROIs; WASSR correction may not fully eliminate this.
  • B1 inhomogeneity from the body coil at 3 T (±30% is typical) means the 0.5 µT saturation field varies across the field of view. The compromise B1 of 0.5 µT undersaturates lactate OH and oversaturates glycogen rNOE, reducing dynamic range. Hepatic glycogen varies with prandial state; the scan should be performed in a standardised fasting state (≥6 h).
  • Respiratory gating adds dead time but is essential. Glucagon reduces peristalsis but may alter pancreatic metabolism. Concentration values for many (ROI, metabolite) pairs are estimates, not direct measurements, and simulation contrast depends critically on these assumed values.
  • [Target tissue not sampled] None of the ROIs (pancreatic body, liver (right lobe), spleen, paraspinal muscle) is inside the target tissue 'pancreas' -- this survived the retry loop, so the plan does not actually verify anything about that tissue.
  • [Not simulated] No reference-backed simulation was possible for: pancreatic body/taurine, liver (right lobe)/taurine, spleen/taurine, paraspinal muscle/taurine, pancreatic body/alanine, liver (right lobe)/alanine, spleen/alanine, paraspinal muscle/alanine, pancreatic body/zinc ions (Zn²⁺) in beta-cell secretory granules, liver (right lobe)/zinc ions (Zn²⁺) in beta-cell secretory granules, spleen/zinc ions (Zn²⁺) in beta-cell secretory granules, paraspinal muscle/zinc ions (Zn²⁺) in beta-cell secretory granules.
  • Their predicted_contrast_percent is reported as 0 (not simulated), not as a prediction.
